content.text: Escaping quotes protects exactly one place in a query: a value inside a quoted string. Numbers, column names, sort directions and data read back from your own database are other places, and escaping does nothing there. Parameterized queries send the SQL text and the values separately, so input can never become code. Use them for every value, and map anything structural to an allow-list.
A pull request adds a "products by category" query. The reviewer asks about SQL injection, and the author points to the helper that doubles every single quote, with tests to prove it:
matches nothing. It gets merged. A week later, a curious customer changes the category in the URL to
, and the page lists every product in the table, including a draft price list that was never published. There isn't a single quote in that input.
is a quoting problem. Escape the quotes in user input, so it can't break out of its string, and the query is safe.
It's half true, which is why it lasts. The textbook attack,
, is made of quotes, and escaping really does defuse it inside a string literal: in our test, the condition became

and matched nothing. Escape functions have been around for a long time, and OWASP's own Top 10 still lists escaping as a fallback: "For any residual dynamic queries, escape special characters using the specific escape syntax for that interpreter." So a team that escapes everything feels covered. The problem is everything that isn't a quoted string.
Injection is code and data sharing one string

OWASP's SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet gives the definition: "SQL injection occurs when untrusted data becomes part of a query's SQL syntax." Its community page names the root cause: "SQL makes no real distinction between the control and data planes." When you build a query by gluing strings together, the database's parser decides which characters are code. Escaping is you trying to predict that parser, for every context, in every dialect.
A number has no quotes to escape. In the story above,

, the filter on published products disappeared. Structure is worse: the A05:2025 Injection page warns that "SQL structures such as table names, column names, and so on cannot be escaped." And escaping isn't even stable for strings: OWASP notes that it "depends on the SQL dialect and configuration", which is why it calls escaping "STRONGLY DISCOURAGED" as a substitute for parameters.
Escaping protects one query, once. The database stores

with its real quote, and the next piece of code that reads it back and glues it into another query is working with raw input again. That's why OWASP says its controls apply "regardless of whether data comes from an HTTP request, another service, or previously stored data."
Parameters keep values out of the SQL text

sends two things: SQL text with placeholders, and the values, each with a type. In OWASP's words, prepared statements "treat bound values as data rather than SQL syntax." The text never changes, whatever the user types, so there's nothing for input to break out of.

-- Escaped, categoryId = "0 OR 1=1": 4 rows, the draft included
SELECT Name, Price FROM Products
WHERE IsPublished = 1 AND CategoryId = 0 OR 1=1

-- Parameterized, categoryId = 2: 2 rows
(@categoryId int)SELECT Name, Price FROM Products
WHERE IsPublished = 1 AND CategoryId = @categoryId

items.text: SQL injection happens when input becomes part of the SQL syntax, not just when it contains quotes.
Escaping protects only quoted strings; numbers, identifiers and stored data slip past it.
Parameters send SQL text and values separately, so the database never parses input as code.
Map column names and sort directions to an allow-list, because parameters can't hold structure.
